did_you_know.text: Did you know? The psalm opens with a series of commands calling people to give thanks to the Lord, call on his name, and proclaim his deeds among the nations.
Did you know? Alongside remembering the wonders and signs, the verse also mentions the judgments of the Lord’s mouth—that is, his words and commands.
Did you know? The psalm emphasizes that the Lord remembers his covenant forever, describing its enduring validity with the phrase “for a thousand generations.”
Did you know? The ancestors are described as initially few in number and strangers in the land, even though the land of Canaan had been promised to them.

Did you know? In the account of the ancestors’ wanderings appears a warning: “Do not touch my anointed ones” and “do my prophets no harm”—an expression of the Lord’s protection of his chosen people and messengers.
Did you know? Joseph is described as being sent ahead of his family to Egypt, even though he actually arrived there as a slave who had been sold.
Did you know? According to the psalm, the king of Egypt released Joseph from prison, after which he became ruler over the royal household and all the king’s possessions.
Did you know? Moses and Aaron are presented as messengers chosen by the Lord to carry out his word in Egypt and perform the signs and wonders.
Did you know? In the wilderness, the Lord’s protection is described as a cloud by day and a fire that gives light by night.
Did you know? The psalm concludes by presenting the purpose of the gifts given to Israel: to keep the Lord’s statutes and teachings, not merely to receive the land.
